questions.question: A support bot's Claude responses sometimes call `lookup_order` with an order number when the user actually asked about refunds. The tool's description is just "Looks up an order." What is the most effective first fix?
options: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} so Claude must pick a tool every turn
Rewrite the description to explain what the tool returns, when to use it, when not to use it (e.g. refund policy questions), and what each parameter means
Rename the tool to `tool_1` so Claude relies on the system prompt instead
Add a system prompt line in capital letters telling Claude never to call tools unless asked
questions.explanation: Tool descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to decide whether and how to call a tool; detailed descriptions covering purpose, usage boundaries and parameters are the highest-leverage fix. Forcing tool use (`any`) would make over-calling worse, and obscure names remove useful signal.

questions.question: A CI job runs a Claude-powered reviewer on every push to a PR, burning tokens on tiny typo commits. Which option reduces cost most sensibly?
options: Review the entire repository on each push
Disable CI entirely
Trigger only on opened/ready-for-review events and skip draft or docs-only changes via path filters, reviewing only the diff
Increase the model size
questions.explanation: Narrow triggers and diff-only review cut cost without losing value. Reviewing the whole repo each time is wasteful.

questions.question: An LLM-generated SQL query is executed directly against a production database by a text-to-SQL feature. Which TWO measures best reduce risk from malicious or erroneous prompts? Select TWO.
options: Connect with a read-only database role limited to the needed schemas/views
Hide the table names from the user interface
Let the model decide whether a query needs approval
Validate or parse the generated SQL and reject statements other than permitted SELECTs
Ask the model to prefix queries with a comment saying they are safe
questions.explanation: Treat model output as untrusted input: least-privilege credentials and server-side validation. Comments, UI hiding and model-decided approval provide no enforcement.

questions.question: A developer interpolates user text into a prompt like `Summarize: {user_text}` and later asks the model to 'follow the user's formatting instructions'. Which change reduces the chance that user text is read as instructions?
options: Remove the system prompt
Increase max_tokens
Clearly delimit user content (e.g., XML tags) and tell the model that content inside the tags is data, while still enforcing risky actions outside the model
Put the user text first in the prompt
questions.explanation: Delimiting and labeling untrusted data helps the model distinguish roles, though it is a mitigation rather than a guarantee, so critical actions need external enforcement.

questions.question: A team wants high confidence in a security-sensitive code review and is willing to pay extra. They run the same review prompt several times with different framing and flag an issue if any run reports it. Which pattern is this?
options: Parallelization with voting
Prompt chaining
Routing
Orchestrator-workers
questions.explanation: Voting runs the same or similar task multiple times to get diverse outputs and raise confidence, here by flagging a finding when any run raises it.

questions.question: A prompt developer iterates by editing the prompt and eyeballing two sample outputs each time. Regressions keep slipping into production. What is the most effective improvement to their process?
options: Add more adjectives to every prompt.
Build a small eval set with expected outcomes and run it on every prompt change so improvements are measured, not guessed.
Ask Claude if the new prompt 'looks better' and trust the answer.
Make prompt changes less often.
questions.explanation: Iterative refinement needs measurement: a regression-style eval set makes changes comparable. Fewer changes does not detect failures, self-assessment without data is unreliable, and adjectives are not a process.

questions.question: Select TWO considerations when writing instructions for models like Claude that follow instructions precisely.
options: Be explicit about the scope: whether to apply a rule to every case or only to certain inputs.
Use contradictory instructions to cover all cases.
Assume the model will infer unstated requirements exactly as you intended.
Provide context for why a rule exists so the model can generalise sensibly.
Rely on emphatic capital letters instead of explanation.
questions.explanation: Giving rationale and explicit scope reduces misinterpretation. Unstated assumptions, contradictions and shouting create ambiguity or over-application.

questions.question: A developer wants a coding agent with built-in file reading, editing, shell commands, and a ready-made agent loop, without implementing tool execution themselves. Which option fits best?
options: The Claude Agent SDK, which exposes the same agent loop and built-in tools used by Claude Code as a library
The Messages API alone, because it runs built-in file and shell tools automatically
A prompt-caching configuration, which provides the tool loop
A Batch API job, which loops over tools until the task is done
questions.explanation: The Agent SDK ships the Claude Code agent loop with built-in tools such as file and shell tools. The plain Messages API returns tool_use blocks that your code must execute.

questions.question: A team's multi-step agent sometimes skips a required validation step. They need the step to happen every time. Which framework-agnostic design is best?
options: Make the step a deterministic node or gate in the harness or workflow rather than relying on the model to choose it
Lower max_tokens to force shorter paths
Mention the step more often in the system prompt
Randomize tool order to cover all cases
questions.explanation: Required steps belong in code (a workflow node or hook), so they cannot be skipped. Prompt emphasis is probabilistic.

questions.question: A tool accepts a `status` argument that must be one of "open", "pending" or "closed". Select TWO. Which practices handle this well?
options: Declare the property with a JSON Schema enum and describe what each value means
Still validate the value in the handler and return an is_error tool_result if it is invalid
Describe the allowed values only in the system prompt
Accept any string and silently fix invalid values in the handler
Use type number and map 1-3 to statuses
questions.explanation: An enum in the input schema puts the constraint where Claude sees it and reduces invalid calls, but the harness should still validate model-produced input and report problems through an is_error result. System-prompt-only constraints, numeric codes and silent fix-ups are weaker.

questions.question: A team's long-running Agent SDK job must capture the full transcript before the SDK compacts the conversation. Which hook fits?
options: PostToolUseFailure
SubagentStart
UserPromptSubmit
PreCompact
questions.explanation: PreCompact fires when compaction is requested, making it the place to archive the full transcript before it is summarized.

questions.question: Which TWO should be recorded as constraints when planning a Claude solution? Select TWO.
options: Required response language(s) and supported regions
The model's internal weights
Budget per 1,000 requests
The exact wording of every future prompt
Whether the model enjoys the task
questions.explanation: Cost ceilings and locale/regional constraints bound the architecture; prompt wording is design detail.

questions.question: A team needs Claude Code to run the same internal linting script with exactly the same flags every time, and they want it to happen automatically after each file edit. What is the best mechanism?
options: An MCP server exposing a lint tool Claude may call
A Skill describing how linting works
A line in CLAUDE.md asking Claude to remember to lint
A hook configured for post-edit events that runs the script deterministically
questions.explanation: Hooks are deterministic, event-driven shell commands executed by the harness, so they happen every time. Instructions in CLAUDE.md or Skills are advisory and an MCP tool still relies on the model deciding to call it.

questions.question: Which TWO statements about recovering a broken stream are correct? Select TWO.
options: Tool use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered, so resume from the most recent complete text block or redo that part of the turn
The server stores undelivered tokens and replays them on reconnect
Setting stream: false guarantees no network interruption occurs
A broken stream is always billed as zero tokens
Successfully received text can be captured and continued with a follow-up request instead of regenerating everything
questions.explanation: The docs state text can be resumed but tool_use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered. The API does not replay undelivered tokens, billing is not guaranteed zero, and non-streaming requests can also fail.

questions.question: Which MCP primitive is designed to be user-controlled, surfacing reusable templates such as a "review this pull request" workflow that a user explicitly selects?
options: Roots
Resources
Prompts
Tools
questions.explanation: MCP prompts are reusable, parameterised message templates that users trigger explicitly (for example as slash commands in Claude Code). Tools are model-invoked and resources are application-attached.

questions.question: Your guardrail pipeline has an input filter, the model's own safety behavior, and an output filter. An auditor asks why all three are needed. What is the best answer?
options: They are redundant, and only the last one matters
Output filters make the other layers unnecessary
Each layer catches different failure modes, so independent layers reduce the chance that a single bypass leads to harm
Layering is only for latency
questions.explanation: Defense in depth assumes any single control can fail; independent layers with different detection methods lower the probability of an end-to-end failure.

questions.question: An invoice-extraction service needs every response to be valid JSON matching a fixed schema. Which approach gives the strongest guarantee on supported models?
options: Ask nicely for JSON in the system prompt and trust it.
Set temperature to 0 and assume the output is always valid.
Use the API's structured outputs feature (output_config.format with a JSON schema) and still validate the result in code.
Parse with a regular expression that grabs anything between braces.
questions.explanation: Structured outputs constrain generation to the schema, and application-side validation covers semantic checks. Politeness, regex scraping and temperature 0 give no schema guarantee.

questions.question: Which practice best prevents an interactive agent from re-reading the same large file repeatedly and filling its context?
options: Ask the user to paste the file into each message.
Read the entire repository once at the start of every session.
Disable file-reading tools after the first read.
Record the relevant findings from the file in a concise working note or memory and refer to it, re-reading only specific sections if needed.
questions.explanation: Notes capture conclusions so large sources need not be reloaded; targeted re-reads cover gaps. Disabling tools blocks progress, reading everything up front bloats context, and pasting just moves the bloat.

questions.question: A team is moving from an older Claude model to a newer one. Which TWO checks are most important before cutting over production traffic? Select TWO.
options: Re-run the evaluation suite to detect behaviour, formatting and quality differences
Read the model's migration notes for breaking API changes such as removed or rejected parameters
Assume prompts behave identically because model names look similar
Increase temperature to compensate for any differences
Skip checks and rely on the provider's average benchmark scores
questions.explanation: Models differ in behaviour and sometimes in supported API parameters, so regression evals and the migration guide are the key gates. Benchmark averages do not capture your tasks.

questions.question: An agent summarises its own previous summaries every 20 turns. After several rounds it has lost a key requirement ('never email customers directly'). What is the best mitigation? Select TWO.
options: Increase temperature to encourage the model to recall hidden details.
Remove the constraint once the summary no longer mentions it.
Keep non-negotiable constraints in the system prompt or a pinned section that is never summarised.
Summarise more frequently so each summary is shorter.
Have the summary template include an explicit 'constraints' field that is carried forward verbatim.
questions.explanation: Repeated lossy summarisation erodes details, so hard constraints must live in pinned, non-summarised locations or fixed template fields. Summarising more often worsens loss, deleting constraints is the failure itself, and temperature does not restore lost text.

questions.question: A team keeps a staging environment that mirrors production. What life-cycle benefit does it provide?
options: Faster models
Safer validation of changes before release
Automatic compliance
Lower token prices
questions.explanation: Staging reduces the chance that defects reach production.

questions.question: A team's agent loop sometimes runs indefinitely when a tool keeps returning ambiguous results. Which TWO architectural safeguards are most appropriate? Select TWO.
options: Add hard limits on iterations, tokens or spend
Raise temperature so the loop eventually breaks out
Rely on the model to decide it has done enough, since it is capable
Define explicit stopping conditions and an escalation path to a human when they are hit
Remove tool results from the context so the model cannot be confused
questions.explanation: Agents are autonomous loops, so they need code-enforced ceilings plus defined stop and escalation behavior. Relying on the model alone to stop is not dependable, and hiding tool results or changing temperature does not bound the loop.

questions.question: A support team streams Claude's answers token by token to a web UI and asks why partial text is available before the full response is finished. Which fact about generation explains this?
options: Claude generates output sequentially, token by token, so the API can stream tokens as they are produced instead of waiting for the full response
Partial text is stored in the prompt cache and replayed to the client
Streaming runs a second, cheaper model that predicts the final answer
The model generates the full answer instantly and the server artificially delays the text
questions.explanation: Autoregressive, token-by-token generation is what makes streaming possible; time to first token and total latency are separate considerations. Streaming does not involve a second model or the cache.

questions.question: A team using Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock notices that the 'opus' alias resolves to an older version than on the Anthropic API, causing inconsistent results between environments. What is the recommended fix?
options: Switch providers daily
Ignore the difference since aliases are identical everywhere
Remove the model setting
Pin the exact provider model or deployment ID with the ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables or the model setting
questions.explanation: Aliases resolve differently per provider, so pinning exact IDs keeps behavior consistent and avoids silent changes when aliases move.

questions.question: A team has a shared internal gateway that all services use to call Claude. Which THREE controls belong at that gateway? Select THREE.
options: Rewriting every response so the model's temperature is increased
Timeouts and bounded retry policy applied consistently to upstream calls
Per-team rate limiting and usage logging that records token counts from responses
Centralized storage and injection of the API key so client services never hold it
Caching API keys in each client service for faster startup
questions.explanation: A gateway is the right place for secret custody, quotas and observability, and consistent resilience policies. Distributing keys to clients defeats the purpose, and altering responses' sampling after the fact is meaningless.

questions.question: An internal tool reuses a large prefix, but calls arrive roughly every 20 minutes, so the default cache keeps expiring. What does the docs-supported option look like?
options: Raise max_tokens
Cache entries never expire, so this cannot happen
Set temperature to 0 to keep the cache alive
Use the longer (1-hour) cache TTL option on the cache breakpoint, accepting its higher write cost
questions.explanation: The default ephemeral cache lasts about 5 minutes (refreshed on hits); an extended 1-hour TTL is available at a higher cache-write price. It pays off only if reuse justifies it.

questions.question: An engineer must decide between hand-rolled HTTP calls and the SDK for a new TypeScript service that will use streaming, tool use and typed responses. Which is the stronger recommendation?
options: Use the official SDK to get typed objects, stream helpers, retries and consistent error classes, reserving raw HTTP for languages or environments without an SDK
Use raw fetch and parse server-sent events manually for maintainability
Use raw fetch calls because the SDK is only for Python
Use an unofficial, OpenAI-compatible shim so the code is portable
questions.explanation: SDKs encapsulate the REST details so you can focus on the application, and they track API changes. Parsing SSE by hand is error-prone and unofficial shims may not support all Claude features.

questions.question: A bank's assistant must refuse to discuss investment advice but answer account-feature questions. What is the best way to express this in a prompt?
options: Tell the model to never answer anything unsure.
Only describe in-scope topics and hope the rest is refused.
Describe both in-scope and out-of-scope topics with a short example of an acceptable refusal and a redirect, in the system prompt.
Say 'Be careful.'
questions.explanation: Explicit scope boundaries with an example of the desired refusal behaviour give consistent handling. Vague caution or only positive scope leave edge cases undefined, and over-refusal harms usefulness.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of semantic versioning for an internal SDK wrapping Claude calls?
options: Consumers can infer from the version number whether an upgrade includes breaking changes
It removes the need for changelogs
It guarantees bug-free releases
It speeds up the API
questions.explanation: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH communicates compatibility expectations; it does not guarantee quality.

questions.question: A refactor extracts a Claude-calling module behind an interface so tests can use a fake. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Dependency inversion/injection to isolate external services and enable deterministic tests
Premature optimization
Tight coupling
Monkey patching in production
questions.explanation: Depending on abstractions lets unit tests avoid network calls and nondeterminism.

questions.question: A tool wants to display Claude's progress in real time while running Claude Code programmatically, processing each event as it arrives. Which output option is most appropriate?
options: Running interactive mode in a pseudo-terminal
The plain text output format
Print mode with the streaming JSON output format
Reading settings.json for changes
questions.explanation: The stream-json output format emits events incrementally, enabling real-time handling, whereas plain text or single JSON returns the final result.

questions.question: A developer has a prefix that is shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length and adds cache_control. What happens, and how can they confirm it?
options: The API returns an error and refuses the request
The request still succeeds but the prefix is not cached; usage shows zero cache creation and read tokens, and the minimum length varies by model so check the docs
The prefix is cached anyway but billed at twice the normal rate
The cache is created and extended automatically to the minimum with padding tokens
questions.explanation: Prompts below the model-specific minimum cacheable length are processed normally without caching and without an error. Check usage.cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens, and consult the docs for the model's minimum.

questions.question: A claims-processing app resends a 40-page policy plus a changing per-user greeting at the start of the system prompt on every call, and costs and latency are high. Which design change helps most?
options: Shorten the policy by deleting clauses
Disable streaming
Place the stable policy content first and the volatile per-user text after it, then use prompt caching on the stable prefix
Move the greeting to the front so it is cached
questions.explanation: Caching works on a stable prefix, so volatile text placed early breaks the cache hit. Putting static content first and marking it cacheable reduces cost and latency.

questions.question: Late in a long Claude Code session, the developer still needs the architectural decisions made earlier but the window is filling with old tool output. Which action fits best?
options: Use /clear, then retype everything from memory
Disable all tools for the rest of the session
Use /compact, optionally with instructions about what to preserve, to summarize history while keeping the key decisions
Restart the shell and hope the session remembers
questions.explanation: /compact replaces the history with a summary and can be steered with focus instructions, retaining decisions while freeing space. /clear would discard the decisions, and the other options do not manage the context.

questions.question: Which stakeholder input is most important for defining data-handling requirements?
options: The model vendor's logo team
Competitors
Marketing only
Security, legal, and compliance teams
questions.explanation: Data-handling rules derive from regulatory and security stakeholders.

questions.question: A team wants Claude Code to be prevented from running `rm -rf` commands via the Bash tool. They write a PreToolUse hook script that detects the pattern. What should the script do to block the call?
options: Exit with code 1 and print a warning to stdout
Exit with code 2 and write the reason to stderr
Exit with code 0 without any output
Sleep until the hook times out
questions.explanation: For PreToolUse, exit code 2 is the blocking error and stderr is fed back as the reason. Exit 1 is a non-blocking error, so the tool call would still proceed, and a timeout does not block by default.

questions.question: A product team wants to cut cost without hurting quality. They propose routing easy requests to a small model and escalating hard ones to a larger model. What must they verify for this design to pay off?
options: That temperature is identical on both models
That the small model has exactly the same tokenizer as the large model
That both models return identical output for every prompt
That a reliable routing signal exists and that measured quality and total cost per completed task (including re-tries and escalations) are better than a single-model baseline
questions.explanation: Routing adds complexity (a router that can be wrong, extra tokens on escalation), so it must be evaluated on total cost per completed task and routing accuracy against a single-model baseline. Models need not share tokenizers, sampling settings or outputs for routing to work.

questions.question: A batch of Claude-generated records is inserted by a worker that crashes midway and restarts. How do you avoid duplicates?
options: Delete the table
Add random sleeps
Use unique keys with upsert semantics so reprocessing the same item yields the same state
Restart from zero and insert again
questions.explanation: Idempotent writes make at-least-once processing safe.

questions.question: A research agent explores hundreds of web pages to answer one question. Its context window fills with raw page content and its reasoning quality degrades. Which architectural change most directly addresses this?
options: Lower the sampling temperature to make reasoning more focused
Delegate page exploration to subagents that work in their own context windows and return only concise findings to the lead agent
Ask the agent to read the pages faster in a single turn
Increase max_tokens so the model can write longer reasoning
questions.explanation: Subagents give context isolation: the verbose intermediate tool output stays in the subagent and only a distilled result reaches the parent, preserving the lead agent's context.

questions.question: A coding agent wants Claude to read files and run tests. Which tool design best follows good practice?
options: Separate, focused tools such as read_file and run_tests with typed parameters, instead of one `do_anything(command: string)` tool
No tools; paste the codebase into the prompt
A single tool accepting arbitrary shell strings with no constraints
One tool per line of source code
questions.explanation: Focused tools with typed inputs are easier for Claude to use correctly and for the harness to validate, log and permission. An unconstrained catch-all tool is harder to secure and describe.

questions.question: While consuming a streamed response containing a tool call, which delta type carries the tool arguments as they are generated?
options: citations_delta
text_delta
input_json_delta containing partial_json fragments
signature_delta
questions.explanation: Tool input is streamed as input_json_delta events with partial JSON strings that you concatenate and parse after the content block stops. Parsing each fragment individually will fail.

questions.question: Which TWO situations are best handled by a rule or CLAUDE.md instruction rather than a hook? Select TWO.
options: Telling Claude the team's preferred naming conventions for new modules
Guaranteeing that `git push --force` can never run
Describing how to run the test suite for this repo
Redacting secrets from every tool output deterministically
Blocking writes to a protected directory with certainty
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is guidance Claude reads and usually follows, ideal for conventions and commands. Guarantees must be enforced deterministically by permissions or hooks.

questions.question: An engineer writes a raw HTTP request to the Messages API in curl and gets an authentication error. Which set of headers is required for a basic request?
options: x-api-key with the API key, anthropic-version with an API version string, and content-type application/json
Only content-type application/json, because the key is passed in the JSON body
x-api-key and a websocket upgrade header
Authorization: Basic with the account email and password, plus a model header
questions.explanation: The Messages API expects the API key in x-api-key, an anthropic-version header, and a JSON content type. Keys are not placed in the body and the API does not use basic auth with account credentials. SDKs set these headers for you.

questions.question: A research-assistant app must show users where each claim came from. The current prompt asks Claude to 'include sources' and users find some links that do not support the claim. Which design is most reliable?
options: Ask Claude to cite from memory and trust the links it produces
Pass the source documents with the citations feature (or structured document IDs) so each claim is tied to retrieved passages the app can verify and link
Increase the model size and keep the prompt
Add a disclaimer under every answer
questions.explanation: Grounding answers in supplied documents with machine-readable citations lets the app link and verify real passages. Free-recalled sources can be fabricated, and disclaimers or a bigger model do not guarantee faithful attribution.

questions.question: A support ticket mentions an API failure 'sometime yesterday'. Which TWO pieces of data most help Anthropic support or your own team trace one failing request? Select TWO.
options: Timestamp, model, and the sanitised request parameters for that call.
The user's browser version.
The total monthly invoice.
The request-id from the response header or error body.
A screenshot of the Console home page.
questions.explanation: The request ID identifies the call precisely, and timestamp, model and request details allow reproduction. Browser version, console screenshots and invoices do not trace a specific request.

questions.question: In LangGraph, what enables a human-in-the-loop workflow to pause, wait for approval and later resume from the same point?
options: A higher temperature that makes the graph wait
Calling the model twice and comparing results
Disabling state so each run starts fresh
A checkpointer that persists the thread's graph state so execution can resume with the same thread_id
questions.explanation: Checkpointers save state per thread, which supports pause and resume, fault tolerance, time travel and conversation continuity.

questions.question: Which scenario is the best fit for a custom (client-side) tool defined in the API rather than a Skill?
options: Claude should adopt a more concise writing style
Claude should follow a code-review rubric
An application must let Claude look up inventory in a private database via the app's own backend
Claude needs a brand voice guide
questions.explanation: Access to private backend data requires an executable function the application controls. Style, voice and rubrics are instructions suited to prompts or Skills.

questions.question: A developer streams tokens to the UI and notices that a response ends abruptly mid-sentence. The final message has stop_reason 'max_tokens'. Which TWO responses are appropriate? Select TWO.
options: Delete the system prompt, because it exhausted the context window
Raise max_tokens (and stream if it is large) or ask for a shorter answer
Check stop_reason and treat the text as truncated rather than complete
Ignore it, since mid-sentence endings are normal formatting
Retry with identical settings, because stop_reason 'max_tokens' means the request was rate limited
questions.explanation: A stop_reason of max_tokens means generation stopped because the output cap was reached, not because the model finished. Applications should check stop_reason and handle truncation by raising max_tokens (streaming for large values) or requesting a more concise answer. It is unrelated to rate limits, and the system prompt is not the cause.

questions.question: A production application calls the API with a model alias that Anthropic periodically re-points. Which practice best fits model version pinning for the app?
options: Use an explicit, specific model ID in configuration and promote a new version only after running your evaluation suite
Let each request choose a model at random
Always use the newest alias so users get the best model
Hard-code the model ID in dozens of source files
questions.explanation: Explicit IDs make behavior reproducible, and gated promotion with evals catches regressions. Centralizing the ID in one config avoids hard-coded duplication.

questions.question: A team sets a very high effort level on all routes of their app after hearing it improves quality. Latency and token costs rise sharply on routine chat requests with no quality gain. What is the best adjustment?
options: Tune effort per route: keep high effort for hard reasoning and agentic tasks, and use lower effort for simple, latency-sensitive chat, validating with an evaluation set
Disable the context window to reduce token use
Switch all routes to zero-shot prompting to lower latency
Keep high effort everywhere, because cost is irrelevant when quality can only improve
questions.explanation: Effort trades thoroughness for tokens and latency; its benefit depends on the workload. Measuring on real traffic and setting effort per route balances quality and cost. Context windows cannot be disabled and zero-shot is a prompting style, not a latency control.

questions.question: A developer asks how the Anthropic SDK handles transient failures by default. Which TWO statements match the documented SDK behavior? Select TWO.
options: The retry count can be configured or disabled with the max_retries option (maxRetries in TypeScript)
It retries forever
It automatically retries transient failures (connection errors, 429, 5xx) with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring retry-after when present
It retries 400 errors until they succeed
It never retries and throws on the first error
questions.explanation: Official SDKs retry transient failures a limited number of times (two by default) and expose max_retries to change it. Retrying 400 errors would never help because the request itself is invalid.

questions.question: A chat UI calls the Messages API with streaming enabled and a tool. The tool_use input arrives as many partial JSON fragments. The first implementation calls JSON.parse on each fragment and crashes. What is the correct approach?
options: Parse each fragment with a lenient regex and execute the tool immediately
Request non-streaming only for the first turn and streaming afterward
Disable the tool and ask for plain text
Accumulate the partial JSON fragments for the content block and parse only once the block is complete
questions.explanation: Tool inputs stream as partial JSON deltas that are only valid JSON when the block finishes; buffer them and parse at the end of the block. Executing on fragments is unsafe, and dropping tools or streaming is unnecessary.

questions.question: In the Claude Agent SDK, a hook should log every file the agent edits to an audit trail after the edit succeeds. Which hook event is the best fit?
options: Notification, because it carries every tool result
PreToolUse, because it runs before the tool and so sees the final result
PostToolUse, matched to the file-editing tools
SubagentStop, because it fires whenever a file changes
questions.explanation: PostToolUse fires after a tool returns, with the tool result, which suits audit logging. PreToolUse runs before the call and cannot see the outcome.
